title: The many faces of Karma
description: From Devanagari to Unicode: why Karma is more than a domain name.

body:
# The many faces of Karma

No important name has only one face. **Karma** appears as ​a figure of myth, a scholarly reconstruction, a piece of material culture, a memory carried across languages, and — most recently — a Unicode domain. This post looks at each ‌face in turn: the name and its roots, the Devanagari original, the reconstructed pronunciation, the mythological record, the symbols and sanctuaries, the cross-cultural afterlife, and the engineering that lets the restored ‌spelling resolve in a browser. Taken together, those faces explain why *karma* was never going to be enough — and why the restored form is worth a domain of its ​own.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Karma
- **ASCII form:** karma
- **Meaning:** "Deed, action"
- **Domain of influence:** Action, Consequence
- **Pantheon:** Sanskrit
- **Restoration:** ASCII-equivalent form
- **Original script:** कर्म (Devanagari)

## Overview

**Karma** (*karma*) — ​Deed, Action, the Law of Consequence · Deed, action — belongs to the Sanskrit tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Action, Consequence". The name means "Deed, action".

**Karma** ​is the law that no deed evaporates: every act plants its seed, and the harvest is the life — and lives — that follow. From a plain Vedic noun for “ritual ​action” it grew into the doctrine that drives Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain cosmology alike: the moral physics by which the universe keeps its books without a bookkeeper.

PuniCodex restores the ​name as **Karma** and serves its temple at [its temple](https://punicodex.com/karma/). The restoration aSCII-equivalent form — a description computed from the displayed form itself. The plain ASCII form *karma* survives as a ‌modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete.

## The Name

The name is attested in Devanagari ​as **कर्म**. Etymologically it means "Deed, action".

The ASCII form *karma* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. ​The Unicode restoration **Karma** recovers the full diacritic detail of the scholarly transliteration directly in the address bar. The restoration aSCII-equivalent form — a description computed from the displayed form ‌itself.

## ​The Original Script

The name is preserved in Devanagari as **कर्म**.

The scholarly transliteration is *Karma*.

The rendering proceeds step by step:

- Sanskrit Karma is written in Devanagari as कर्म
- ‌IAST transliteration maps each Devanagari vowel and consonant to a Latin equivalent
- Macrons mark long vowels (ā, ī, ū); dots beneath consonants mark retroflex articulation (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ, ṣ)

## Pronunciation

The ​reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/ˈkɑːrmə/** — Sanskrit (IAST: Karma).

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **Kar-** — From √kṛ, “to do, make”; the r is syllabic-flavoured, the a long “ah”.
- **-ma** ‌— The abstract noun: “action”, “deed” — and by extension, the law that deeds breed consequences.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: “KAHR-muh”

Kindred and historical forms of the ​name:

- **Pali** — Kamma
- **the** — law of moral causation across all Indian traditions

The word begins as a plain noun — “deed” — and becomes the engine of the ​universe. The neuter gender marks the noun as a principle, not a person.

## Mythology

Karma has no biography because it outranks every biography: it is the rule all biographies obey. Its ​‘mythology’ is the doctrine’s own history — from the Vedic ritual’s power to bind, through the Upaniṣads’ interiorization, to the great vehicles’ global export — and the countless stories, from ​Nala to Savitri, in which its arithmetic drives the plot.

### From Ritual to Moral Physics (Upaniṣadic Revolution)

The Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad relocates karma: no longer the ritual act alone but the intention ​behind every act — ‘one becomes good by good action, evil by evil action’. The ritual economy of the Brahmins became the moral economy of the universe, and no priest ‌was needed to run it.

### The Owner of the Deed (Buddhist Formulation)

The Buddha’s formula is the doctrine’s cleanest statement: beings are the owners of their deeds, the heirs of their ​deeds — nowhere else does the inheritance come from. Karma in Buddhism is intention (cetanā) itself; the deed’s fruit follows like the wheel follows the ox.

### The Story Where It ‌Breaks (Savitri Cycle)

The Mahābhārata’s Savitrī tale stages the doctrine’s limit-case: Satyavān’s life exhausted by karma’s count, Yama arrives on schedule — and the wife’s flawless speech wins the husband back. ​The epic never denies the law; it shows a love so exact in its dharma that the law’s own keeper must honour it.

### The Subtle Dust (Jain Mechanics)

Jainism made ‌karma physical: a subtle matter that clings to the soul like dust to a wet cloth, weighing it into rebirth. The doctrine’s imagery — the soul’s lightness restored by austerity until ​it rises like a flame released — is the most materialist eschatology India produced.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography associated with Karma concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, ‌each a compressed statement about the name:

- **The Seed and the Fruit** — Every deed is a seed; the fruit may ripen in this life or a later one — but ​it ripens.
- **Action by Mind, Word, Deed** — Karma accrues by thought, speech, and body — the three doors of action the law watches.
- **The Burning Off** — Karma can ‌be exhausted by experience — burned like a field of stubble — or bound by attachment like a new seed.
- **Liberation Beyond It** — Mokṣa, nirvāṇa: the states beyond karma’s reach ​— the doctrines’ common horizon.

## Archaeology & Evidence

The material record for Karma survives in a small number of securely identified remains, catalogued below; the corpus is thin but unambiguous, ​and each site is tied to the name by ancient testimony.

Karma leaves no temple — it is the reason temples leave merit. The stūpas’ circumambulation-paths, the ghāṭs’ staircases into the ‌rivers, and the endless charity-inscriptions of Indian epigraphy are its monuments: every recorded gift is a seed on record.

## Realm & Domain

**Karma** is the law that no deed evaporates: ‌every act plants its seed, and the harvest is the life — and lives — that follow. From a plain Vedic noun for “ritual action” it grew into the doctrine that ‌drives Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain cosmology alike: the moral physics by which the universe keeps its books without a bookkeeper.

Every deed is a seed; ​the fruit may ripen in this life or a later one — but it ripens.

## Across Cultures

Karma is the one doctrine shared by Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain without alteration of ​name — the subcontinent’s common physics. The West received it through theosophy and thence into the global vernacular, where ‘karma’ now means cosmic payback in any language; classical comparisons run ​to the Egyptian heart-weighing and the Greek Adrasteia.

Within the Sanskrit tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[aditi|Aditi]], [[agni|Agni]], [[ambika|Ambikā]], [[amsa|Aṃśa]], [[arjuna|Arjuna]], and [[bhakti|Bhakti]].

## Cultural Legacy

The word entered ‌every major language as a loan — among the few Sanskrit terms to do so. It underwrites the theory of rebirth, the ethics of non-harm (the deed’s victim returns as ​one’s debtor), and the quietist strand of Indian political thought: the revolution you cannot make today, your karma will make eventually.

## A Meditation

Karma: the plainest noun in the batch — ‘deed’ — carrying ​the heaviest doctrine. Restored without marks, it reads as it acts: no ornament, no exemption, no appeal. The lexicon’s other names guard temples; this one guards the law the temples ‌were built to honour.

## ‌A Closer Look at the Marks

A restored name is a small map. In the case of **Karma**, the map does not lead through diacritics or special letters, because the source ​tradition wrote the name in Devanagari rather than in the Latin alphabet. The ASCII form *karma* and the restored form share the same letters; the restoration is a decision about ​which conventional spelling should serve as the public reference.

That decision is not cosmetic. The original script attestation carries semantic and phonetic information that no romanization can fully reproduce. By fixing ​one conventional spelling as the canonical domain form, the project prevents the drift that happens when a name is romanized differently in every article, map, and database. The breakdown still ‌lists each character — **k**, **a**, **r**, **m**, **a** — so visitors can see exactly what is being carried forward and what is not. What looks like "no change" is, in ​fact, a deliberate choice to keep the name stable, searchable, and addressable.

## Karma in Its Tradition

**Karma** does not stand alone. It belongs to the Sanskrit tradition, where it is ​counted among 102 names in the PuniCodex lexicon. Its sphere — Action, Consequence — places it beside other figures who govern similar aspects of experience. The restored spelling is therefore not ​only a philological decision; it is a way of keeping the name in the company of its kin. When the address bar shows **Karma**, it marks the boundary between a ‌generic search term and a named entry in a living catalog of myth. That catalog is the point of the project. Every restored name is a vote for specificity: the web ​should know the difference between a figure and a keyword, between a tradition and a trend. **Karma** is one such vote.

## The Restoration on the Live Web

A domain name is a kind of publication. When **Karma** resolves, it proves that the restored spelling is not ​a theoretical exercise; it is a working address on the public internet. Search engines can index it, language models can encounter it, and anyone who copies it from a manuscript ‌can paste it into a browser. That practical reality changes the status of the restoration. Before Unicode domains, a scholar could write the name correctly in an article while the public ​web flattened it to *karma*. Now the public web can carry the correct form end to end. The punycode translation happens silently, so the infrastructure remains compatible while the visible ‌name keeps its marks. That compromise — human-readable restoration, machine-readable encoding — is the foundation of every PuniCodex temple.

## Restoration Notes

Restoring a name is not a single decision; it is ‌a sequence of smaller decisions, each backed by a different kind of evidence. For **Karma**, the chain begins with the attested form in Devanagari, continues through the standard scholarly romanizations, ​and ends with the DNS-compatible Unicode spelling used by this temple. The meaning "Deed, action" anchors the name in its semantic field; without that anchor, the marks would float free of ​the figure they name. The restored form **Karma** and the ASCII form *karma* share the same Latin letters; the restoration here is a conventional capitalization rather than a recovery of ​lost diacritics or special characters. Those adjustments are not arbitrary styling. They follow the restoration logic the displayed form wears openly: Karma aSCII-equivalent form. The rule is mechanical, not editorial, which ​means the same standard applies to every entry in the lexicon. A visitor who disagrees with the classification can at least see exactly which evidence produced it, because every step ‌is recorded in the Scholarly Edition. That transparency is the difference between a restoration project and a branding exercise. The name is being put back, not invented.
